en: Then Kanykey, the woman in mourning,
Was sorely troubled in her heart;
Then tears poured from her eyes.
Wailing, weeping, beating herself,
To her mother, the honored elder woman,
Chyiyrdy, she pleaded:
“Ah, my dear mother,
We camped beside the river, ah!
Parted from my precious one,
Mother, we are like a fire put out!
Mother, an iron net has fallen about our feet;
Mother, heavy misfortune has met our brow!
From the dark ridge and ravine
The time has come to turn away.
From the child left by the khan and prince,
Mother, the time has come to part!
Your hoof left behind by the noble steed,
Your lamp left by your son, the splendid warhorse!
Mother, your soft little gray hawk,
If he lives safely and grows up,
Your pale, mottled falcon, your morning star!
Your hoof left behind by the noble steed,
Your little one left by your son, the splendid warhorse,
Your pennant fastened to a spear,
Your gift left by your generous son!
My dear mother, ah,
They will trample upon our heads, I fear;
They will scatter the four kinds of livestock, I fear!
Your descendant left by the precious one,
Semetey, they will seize and slaughter, I fear;
The lamp left behind by the falcon,
The scoundrels will kill him, I fear.
God will strike those dogs, I think;
They will plunder the gold and live at ease, I fear!
Your lamp left behind by the falcon,
Your soft, pale-mottled female goshawk,
If he lives safely and grows up,
Your gray saker, your falcon.
Your hoof left behind by the noble steed,
From your son, the splendid warhorse,
Your little one left by the noble steed.
Your pennant fastened to a spear,
Your gift left by the generous one.
Slaughtering your only one,
Mother, they will leave us like a fire put out, I fear!
The child still in the nursing cradle—
Unless we take care and find a way,
Mother, they will wrench him from your arms, I fear!
Dragging him onto the road,
Mother, they will have the great dogs tear him, I fear!
Mother, that dear bird, the wild duck,
Flies toward the open plain without turning back.
How much must we endure,
Mother, for the child born from the womb?
That wretched bird, the harrier,
Swoops toward the open plain.
We shall perish,
Mother, for the child born from the belly.
We were a gorge; we have become a road.
Mother, parted from your khanly son,
We were princes; we have been humbled.
Mother, we were a vast lake; we have ebbed away.
Mother, when your son was alive,
We took lions from many places.
It was God's decree—
In the end, we devoured your son.
We poor souls who would not drink fermented mare's milk
Now long even for brackish water.
Mother, at the spur where the mountains end,
Mother, at the promontory of the level mountain,
On the face of broad Ak-Chiy,
At the edge of the main road,
Mother, there is your son's little enclosure;
Take shelter in that enclosure!
The camel calf left by your son,
Mother, clasp him to your breast, I beg!
The black cliff of Uyurulmo,
The great mountain lying motionless—
Mother, flee toward it, I beg!
Your child, like a rounded stone,
Clasp him to your breast, I beg!
Deceive them and keep out of sight;
Carry your only one away, I beg!
Your only one, gained at the brink of death,
Mother, clasp him to your breast, I beg!
If the six scoundrels come, they will do no good;
Mother, they will not leave your only one unharmed!
My dear mother,
May you attain your hope;
The only child in your arms,
Take him into Talas and hide him;
Lie at your sacred tomb, I beg;
Without letting the six scoundrels see,
Carry your child away and flee, I beg!
Mother, conceal yourself along the Talas;
Mother, carry your only one to safety!
Conceal yourself along the Ken-Kol;
Mother, their evil will touch him;
Death will come to him like this.
Mother, take your orphan to safety!
Enter Budurmak and take shelter;
It is God's decree.
Mother, if you let him be taken, it will bring disgrace.
My mother and my orphan—
Oh God, I entrust them to you alone!”
Wailing and weeping in sobs,
“Carry him away!” said Kanykey,
Pleading with her mother Chyiyrdy;
She stood there weeping and sobbing.
Then Chyiyrdy stood and said:
“Your falcon mother Chyiyrdy—
While this poor old one watches,
Your slaves cannot seize my orphan.
Dear one, I would merely look this way,
And those scoundrels, each from his horse,
Would fall and lie shattered.
I shall satisfy my longing, I think;
My foal, the orphan child,
I shall clasp him to my breast!
No one can come near me;
Kanykey, my child, no one can meet my eyes!
No man, even a lion, will approach;
Not one of those villains will come near me!”
“Oh, dark day, mother, what are you saying?
Alas, mother, what are you saying?!
When those six scoundrels stared wide-eyed
And fell from their horses—
Mother, that was while your precious one was alive.
Their not coming near you,
Their not looking upon your fair face—
Mother, it was the six scoundrels' deceit.
Better, mother,
Carry away this child left by the generous one!
Mother, your strength is beyond compare;
He who gave his hand to twelve saints,
Your saintly son, is not here.
You have no support on whom to rely;
Mother, you have no secure place to stay.
He before whom they fell when he advanced,
Your renowned lion Manas is gone!”
Chyiyrdy, who had reached eighty,
The orphan, like a rounded stone,
Pressed to her breast as she wailed.
Sobbing and weeping, heading toward the mountain,
Your mother walked along in tears.
Coughing heavily again and again,
Her orphan left by Manas,
Chyiyrdy, enduring hardship,
Lifted and carried him upon her neck.
Her soles were battered by stones;
Her forehead was scorched by the sun;
The flesh about her ankles grew sore.
Your mother's calves ached;
Your mother had no sheltered bank to lie beneath;
Your mother had no food to eat.
Without overshoes, in her stockings,
The poor soul suffered.
Without boots, in her stockings—
Unless the Almighty himself wills it,
It is so hard for the poor soul to die.
Unable to make her way over the ridge,
Your mother could find no room in a familiar place.
For the child born of the hero,
Your mother could not lie down where she headed.
Walking the rolling hills, her strength failed;
Then life drained from your mother Chyiyrdy.
Unable to walk along Chatkal,
Your mother Chyiyrdy
Could not cross Chatkal's ridge;
Exhausted, weeping, unable to walk,
Your mother Chyiyrdy
Could not cross Buura's Pass.
Then, sobbing and weeping, unable to walk,
Coughing heavily again and again,
Your mother, now grown old,
The child like a rounded stone
Carried pressed against her breast.
Among Kyrchyndy's ridged rocks,
Your mother struggled, unable to walk.
In Kaiypchy's Black Cave
Your mother lay in hiding.
She made the cave her home.
It sorely tormented her wretched soul;
It terribly troubled her thoughts.
Chyiyrdy took as her hope
The child still in the nursing cradle.
“That dear bird, the wild duck,
Turns and flies toward the open plain.
Now that I have grown old,
It seems I shall die without burial,
All for the child born from my womb.
The thistles growing on the plain—
Gnawing them, I, the wretched one, shall die.
Parted from my dear people,
I, the wretched one, shall die like this!
The treasure I gathered in gold
I shall scatter and die.
When my foal Manas has died,
Now that I have grown old,
I, the wretched one, shall die in flight.
Where no vulture flaps its wings,
In such a place I shall die.
With no profession of faith called aloud,
I, the wretched one, shall die in the wilderness!”
Chyiyrdy wept and wailed;
From wounded pride she wished to die.
The chief reason she stayed alive
Was that her little Semetey remained.
“Parted from my Manas,
Wandering into Marghalan,
What hope shall I attain!
At this time of journeying,
With my temples white,
Throughout my journey,
I, the wretched one, have roamed and strayed.
What hope shall I attain?
Here, this wretched soul—
Let me become a sacrifice, then!
If you, God, created me as a soul,
Allah Most High, the one God,
Grant a gracious decree.
Gabriel, taker of souls,
Reach out your five fingers to me;
Angel Gabriel,
I have lost my accomplished Manas;
Cut short this life!”
She wailed in supplication.
It was God's decree;
Your mother, in her old age,
Kept lamenting and sobbing.
She had no strength to walk;
Her rib bones came apart.
Your aged mother Chyiyrdy
Had no means of moving.
Tears poured from her eyes;
She could not stop her running nose,
Could not wipe away her tears.
The bright blade with its striped neck
She drew from its sheath
And thought, “Now let me die.”
Then Semetey, still an infant in the cradle,
Reached out with his little hands;
He grasped the old woman's knife,
Reached his hand toward her breast,
And laughed with his mouth wide open.
“My distress is beyond description.
My back broken, night fallen,
As I weep in agony,
This misfortune fallen upon my head,
As I wail in anguish,
The old woman has no good fortune.
To help me over the ridge,
My hero Bakai is not here either.”
Crying out her sorrow,
Your precious mother doubled over;
With no strength to move,
